title: count the solutions of a trigonometric equation with a changed input coefficient on an interval, avoiding lost or extra
stem: How many solutions does the equation 2 sin(3x) = √3 have on the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Let u = 3x, so 0 ≤ u < 6π, three full cycles. sin u = √3/2 has two solutions per cycle (π/3 and 2π/3 plus multiples of 2π), so 2 × 3 = 6 solutions.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Solving sin x = √3/2 gives only 2 solutions, but 3x runs through three full cycles on this interval, so this count is far too small.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: One solution per cycle is counted, but sin u = √3/2 has two solutions in every cycle (u = π/3 and u = 2π/3), so this is half the true count.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This lets 3x run to 12π instead of 6π, doubling the number of cycles, so the count is twice too large.

title: count the solutions of a trigonometric equation with a changed input coefficient on an interval, avoiding lost or extra  (variant 1)
stem: How many solutions does the equation 2 cos(2x) = −1 have on the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Solving cos x = −1/2 gives 2 solutions, but 2x runs through two full cycles, so the count must double.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Let u = 2x, so 0 ≤ u < 4π, two full cycles. cos u = −1/2 has two solutions per cycle (2π/3 and 4π/3), so 2 × 2 = 4 solutions (x = π/3, 2π/3, 4π/3, 5π/3).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This counts four solutions per cycle of 2x, but cos u = −1/2 has only two solutions per cycle (2π/3 and 4π/3).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This drops one of the four solutions as if it fell outside the interval, but x = π/3, 2π/3, 4π/3 and 5π/3 all lie in [0, 2π).

title: count the solutions of a trigonometric equation with a changed input coefficient on an interval, avoiding lost or extra  (variant 2)
stem: How many solutions does the equation sin(4x) = 1 have on the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses two solutions per cycle, as for most values of sine, but sin u = 1 occurs only once per cycle (u = π/2), at the top of the wave.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Let u = 4x, so 0 ≤ u < 8π, four full cycles. sin u = 1 has exactly one solution per cycle (u = π/2 + 2πk), so 4 solutions (x = π/8, 5π/8, 9π/8, 13π/8).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This solves sin x = 1 only (one solution per cycle) and forgets that 4x runs through four cycles.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This multiplies by 4 twice, once for the cycles and once for the coefficient, giving four times the true count.

title: count the solutions of a trigonometric equation with a changed input coefficient on an interval, avoiding lost or extra  (variant 3)
stem: How many solutions does the equation cos(3x) = 1/2 have on the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ π?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This treats 3x as covering three full cycles, but 0 ≤ 3x ≤ 3π is only one and a half cycles.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This counts only the two solutions in the first cycle (u = π/3 and 5π/3) and ignores that 3x continues past 2π to 7π/3.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: Let u = 3x, so 0 ≤ u ≤ 3π. cos u = 1/2 at u = π/3, 5π/3 and 7π/3 (the next, 11π/3, exceeds 3π), so there are 3 solutions.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This lets 3x run to 4π instead of 3π, which picks up solutions at 11π/3 that lie outside the interval.

title: solve a trigonometric inequality on an interval, keeping every arc and reversing the inequality when dividing by a negat
stem: On the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π, which gives the complete solution set of 2cos x + 1 > 0?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is where cos x < −1/2; the inequality sign was reversed, so it gives the region the inequality excludes.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: 2cos x + 1 > 0 gives cos x > −1/2. Cosine equals −1/2 at 2π/3 and 4π/3 and is larger outside the arc between them, so x is in [0, 2π/3) ∪ (4π/3, 2π).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This solves cos x > 1/2 by using the reference angle π/3 and ignoring the sign, but the inequality is cos x > −1/2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This keeps only the part near 0 and loses the symmetric piece (4π/3, 2π) where cosine is also greater than −1/2.

title: solve a trigonometric inequality on an interval, keeping every arc and reversing the inequality when dividing by a negat (variant 1)
stem: On the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π, which gives the complete solution set of sin x ≤ −√2/2?

choices.rationale: This is where sin x ≥ −√2/2; the inequality direction was reversed, so it describes the complement of the solution set.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This solves sin x ≥ √2/2 and drops the negative sign, so the arc lies in the upper half of the circle where sine is positive.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses the endpoints where sin x = −1/2 (reference angle π/6) instead of −√2/2 (reference angle π/4).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: sin x = −√2/2 at 5π/4 and 7π/4, and sine is at or below that value between them (down to −1 at 3π/2), so x is in [5π/4, 7π/4].

title: solve a trigonometric inequality on an interval, keeping every arc and reversing the inequality when dividing by a negat (variant 2)

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: 2sin x > 1 gives sin x > 1/2. Sine equals 1/2 at π/6 and 5π/6 and exceeds it between them, so x is in (π/6, 5π/6).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses the angles where sin x = √3/2 instead of 1/2, so it cuts off part of the solution set.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This stops at π/2, losing the portion (π/2, 5π/6) in the second quadrant where sine is still greater than 1/2.

title: solve a trigonometric inequality on an interval, keeping every arc and reversing the inequality when dividing by a negat (variant 3)

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This reverses the inequality correctly but drops the negative sign, solving cos x < √3/2.

choices.label: D

title: find the range of a transformed secant or cosecant function by combining the |value| ≥ 1 restriction with a stretch, ref
stem: What is the range of the function y = 2csc x − 1?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: csc x ≤ −1 or csc x ≥ 1. Doubling gives ≤ −2 or ≥ 2, and subtracting 1 gives y ≤ −3 or y ≥ 1, so the range is (−∞, −3] ∪ [1, ∞).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This treats csc x like a bounded wave with values between −1 and 1; the cosecant takes every value with magnitude at least 1, so it is unbounded.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This applies the vertical stretch by 2 but forgets the shift down by 1.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This shifts the stretched range up by 1 instead of down by 1.

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

title: find the range of a transformed secant or cosecant function by combining the |value| ≥ 1 restriction with a stretch, ref (variant 2)
stem: What is the range of the function y = −2csc x + 1?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This treats the values between the two branches as attained, but |csc x| ≥ 1, so the stretched and shifted function never takes values between −1 and 3 and is unbounded.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: csc x ≤ −1 or csc x ≥ 1, so −2csc x ≥ 2 or ≤ −2 (a reflection keeps the same two pieces). Adding 1 gives y ≤ −1 or y ≥ 3, so the range is (−∞, −1] ∪ [3, ∞).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This shifts the range down by 1 instead of up by 1; the reflection does not change the symmetric set of magnitudes ≥ 2.

choices.label: D

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This forgets the vertical compression and uses magnitudes of at least 1, then shifts down by 3.

stem: On the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ π, at which x-values does the graph of y = csc(2x − π/3) have vertical asymptotes?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Asymptotes occur where sin(2x − π/3) = 0, so 2x − π/3 = kπ and x = π/6 + kπ/2. In [0, π] this gives k = 0 and k = 1: x = π/6 and x = 2π/3 (k = 2 gives 7π/6, outside the interval).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This solves 2x + π/3 = kπ, shifting the wrong way, so every asymptote lands π/3 away from the true location.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This gives the zeros of sin(2x), ignoring the phase shift of π/3 inside the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This finds the first asymptote but steps by π instead of π/2 between asymptotes, forgetting that 2x halves the spacing.

stem: The polar function r = 4sin θ − 2 is graphed for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. On which interval(s) of θ does the plotted point get closer to the pole (its distance from the origin decreases)?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: r' = 4cos θ and r = 0 at θ = π/6 and 5π/6. Distance decreases when r and r' have opposite signs: r < 0 and r' > 0 on (0, π/6); r > 0 and r' < 0 on (π/2, 5π/6). So the point approaches the pole on (0, π/6) ∪ (π/2, 5π/6).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is where r is increasing, but r is positive on part of it, where an increasing r moves the point away from the pole.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is where the distance increases (r positive and increasing, or r negative and decreasing), the opposite of what is asked.

stem: A polar function r = f(θ) is continuous and strictly increasing on [π/6, π/2], with f(π/6) = −2 and f(π/2) = 4. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The average rate of change of r is 18/π per radian, and the distance of the plotted point from the pole increases throughout the interval.
choices.rationale: This finds the rate correctly but claims the distance increases throughout, reading the increase in r as a move away from the pole even where r is negative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average rate of change of r is 18/π per radian, and the distance of the plotted point from the pole decreases throughout the interval.
choices.rationale: This finds the rate correctly but claims the distance decreases throughout, ignoring that r becomes positive and then moves farther from the pole.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The average rate of change of r is 18/π per radian, and the distance of the plotted point from the pole first decreases to 0 and then increases.
choices.rationale: Correct: The average rate of change is (4 − (−2))/(π/2 − π/6) = 6/(π/3) = 18/π. Since r is continuous and increasing from −2 to 4, it passes through 0 once: |r| falls from 2 to 0 and then rises to 4.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average rate of change of r is 6/π per radian, and the distance of the plotted point from the pole first decreases to 0 and then increases.
choices.rationale: This finds the change in distance, (4 − 2)/(π/3), instead of the change in r itself, (4 − (−2))/(π/3); the average rate of change is for r, signed.

stem: A polar function r = f(θ) is continuous and strictly decreasing on [π/6, π/2], with f(π/6) = −1 and f(π/2) = −7. Which statement is correct?
